DETAILED ACTION
Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Remarks
This communication is in response to Application No. 18/236,263 filed on 08/21/2023.
Claims 1-20 are currently pending and have been examined.
Drawings
The drawings filed 08/21/2023 are acceptable.
Claim Interpretation Under 35 USC § 112
No claim elements in this application are presumed to invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f).
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(d):
(d) REFERENCE IN DEPENDENT FORMS.—Subject to subsection (e), a claim in dependent form shall contain a reference to a claim previously set forth and then specify a further limitation of the subject matter claimed. A claim in dependent form shall be construed to incorporate by reference all the limitations of the claim to which it refers.
The following is a quotation of pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, fourth paragraph:
Subject to the following paragraph [i.e., the fifth paragraph of pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112], a claim in dependent form shall contain a reference to a claim previously set forth and then specify a further limitation of the subject matter claimed. A claim in dependent form shall be construed to incorporate by reference all the limitations of the claim to which it refers.
Claim 12 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(d) or pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, 4th paragraph, as being of improper dependent form for failing to further limit the subject matter of the claim upon which it depends, or for failing to include all the limitations of the claim upon which it depends.
Claim 12 merely recites the last clause of claim 11 and thus fails to further limit the subject matter of the claim upon which it depends.
Applicant may cancel the claim(s), amend the claim(s) to place the claim(s) in proper dependent form, rewrite the claim(s) in independent form, or present a sufficient showing that the dependent claim(s) complies with the statutory requirements.
NOTE: any prior art rejection provided below is made as best understood in view of the 35 U.S.C. 112(b) issues above.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(a)(1) the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
(a)(2) the claimed invention was described in a patent issued under section 151, or in an application for patent published or deemed published under section 122(b), in which the patent or application, as the case may be, names another inventor and was effectively filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
References cited in this section:
D1 - US 2017/0268345 A1
D3 – US 11,905,847 (filed 21 Oct. 2022)
Claims 1-8 and 16-19  are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) and/or 102(a)(2) as being anticipated by D1.
As to claim 1, D1 discloses a CMC component (figs. 2-3)  for a gas turbine engine  (fig. 1) comprising:
an airfoil (at least one airfoil 102) comprising:
a leading edge (114 in figs. 4-5);
a trailing edge (116);
a suction sidewall (120); and
a pressure sidewall (118) comprising a locally-thickened region (thicker portion 140 in fig. 5), the locally-thickened region (140) being a maximum thickness region of the pressure sidewall (fig. 5), wherein the locally-thickened region has a first thickness (fig. 5 shows thickness);
wherein a maximum thickness region (thinner portion 142 in fig. 4) of the suction sidewall (120) has a second thickness (142); and
wherein the first thickness (thicker portion 140) is greater than the second thickness (thinner portion 142; it is noted that 140 appears greater than 142).

As to claim 2, D1 discloses the component of claim 1, and further discloses wherein the first thickness is up to 30% greater than the second thickness ([0034] 10% to 150% range disclosed).
As to claim 3, D1 discloses the component of claim 1, and further discloses wherein the locally-thickened region (thicker portion 140 in figs. 3 and 5) is disposed between 0% and 50% span of the airfoil (fig. 3 shows 140 between 0% and 50% span).
As to claim 4, D1 discloses the component of claim 1, and further discloses wherein the locally-thickened region is disposed between and 50% span and 100% span of the airfoil (fig. 5 shows another 140 between 50% and 100% span as the thick/thin is periodic from 106 to 104).
As to claim 5, D1 discloses the component of claim 1 and further comprising:
a first platform (one of 104 and 106 in fig. 3); and
a second platform (the other of 104 and 106 in fig. 3),
wherein the airfoil (103) is connected to and extends between the first platform and the second platform (fig. 3).
As to claim 6, D1 discloses the component of claim 5, and further discloses wherein the component is a vane ([0019] the type of component, e.g., rotating blade, stator vane).
As to claim 7, D1 discloses the component of claim 5, and further discloses wherein the pressure sidewall comprises a first subset of plies ([0033] In certain embodiments, the airfoil wall 122 is generally formed from a plurality of plies 152, as shown in FIG. 6. However, in the hot zone 150 (i.e., where the thermal load is applied during use) includes additional plies 154 on the airfoil inner surface 103 such that the thicker section 150 corresponds to a contour on the airfoil inner surface 103. That is, additional plies 154 are placed on  the inner surface 103 to form the thicker section 140 in the hot area 150. However, the contour of the outer surface 103).
As to claim 8, D1 discloses the component of claim 7, and further discloses wherein the locally-thickened region comprises at least one additional ply ([0033] In certain embodiments, the airfoil wall 122 is generally formed from a plurality of plies 152, as shown in FIG. 6. However, in the hot zone 150 (i.e., where the thermal load is applied during use) includes additional plies 154 on the airfoil inner surface 103 such that the thicker section 150 corresponds to a contour on the airfoil inner surface 103. That is, additional plies 154 are placed on  the inner surface 103 to form the thicker section 140 in the hot area 150).

As to claim 16, D1 discloses a vane assembly (fig. 2) for a gas turbine engine (fig. 1), the vane assembly comprising:
an inner case (the engine of fig. 1 has an inner case, shown but not numbered);
an outer case (the engine of fig. 1 has an outer case, shown but not numbered); and
at least one CMC vane (at least one airfoil 102) coupled between the inner case and the outer case (fig. 2), the at least one CMC vane comprising:
an inner diameter platform (106 in fig. 3);
an outer diameter platform (104 in fig. 3); and
an airfoil (at least one airfoil 102) connected to and extending between the inner diameter platform and the outer diameter platform (fig. 2), the airfoil comprising:
a leading edge (114 in figs. 4-5);
a trailing edge (116);
a suction sidewall (120); and
a pressure sidewall (118) comprising a locally-thickened region (thicker portion 140 in fig. 5) extending from the inner diameter platform or the outer diameter platform toward a midspan region pressure sidewall (fig. 3), the locally-thickened region being a maximum thickness region of the pressure sidewall (figs. 4 and 5), wherein the locally-thickened region has a first thickness (fig. 5 shows thickness);
wherein a maximum thickness region (thinner portion 142 in fig. 4) of the suction sidewall (120) has a second thickness (142); and
wherein the first thickness (thicker portion 140) is greater than the second thickness (thinner portion 142; it is noted that 140 appears greater than 142).
As to claim 17, D1 discloses the assembly of claim 16, wherein the first thickness is 30% greater than the second thickness (see explanation for claim 2).
As to claim 18, D1 discloses the assembly of claim 17, and further discloses wherein the pressure sidewall comprises a first subset of plies (fig. 6 shows ply construction of the airfoil).
As to claim 19, D1 discloses the assembly of claim 18, and further discloses wherein the locally-thickened region (thicker portion 140 in fig. 6) comprises at least one additional ply (154).
Claims 10-13 and 15 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) and/or 102(a)(2) as being anticipated by D3.

As to claim 10, D3 discloses a method of forming a CMC component, the method comprising:
identifying stress regions in the component exceeding a threshold value (col. 5, ln. 55 through col. 6, ln. 5, placing thickened regions to accommodate thermal stress implicitly requires determining stress regions);
subsequently, forming a preform by:
laying up a first subset of plies over a mandrel (a method of forming the airfoil 60. As shown in FIG. 8, fiber plies 64a are laid-up around a plurality of mandrels 72);
laying up at least one reinforcing ply over the first subset of plies, the at least one reinforcing ply coextensive with the stress regions (col. 7, lns. 14-29, the ceramic fiber plies 64a are used to locally build-up the thickness which provides improved cooling at areas of high thermal stress); and
laying up a second subset of plies over the at least one reinforcing ply (col. 7, lns. 14-29); and
densifying the preform with a ceramic matrix (col. 2, lns. 50-55, the forming includes i) fabricating a fiber preform of the airfoil around a plurality of mandrels, wherein the mandrel in the first sub-cavity is radially split, and ii) densifying the fiber preform with a ceramic matrix).
As to claim 11, D3 discloses the method of claim 10, and further discloses wherein the first subset of plies and the second subset of plies define an airfoil (fig. 4), the airfoil comprising:
a leading edge (62a);
a trailing edge (62b);
a suction sidewall (62d); and
a pressure sidewall (62c),
wherein the at least one reinforcing ply is disposed along the pressure sidewall between 0% span and 50% span (span S in fig. 4 shows 0-100% and fig. 5 shows additional plies at approximately 0-50 and 50-100%; see fig. 5).
As to claim 12, D3 discloses the method of claim 11, and further discloses wherein the at least one reinforcing ply is disposed along the pressure sidewall between 0% span and 50% span (span S in fig. 4 shows 0-100% and fig. 5 shows additional plies at approximately 0-50 and 50-100%; see fig. 5).
As to claim 13, D3 discloses the method of claim 11, and further discloses wherein the at least one reinforcing ply is disposed along the pressure sidewall between 50% span and 100% span (fig. 5).
As to claim 15, D3 discloses the method of claim 10, and further discloses wherein the step of densifying the preform with a ceramic matrix comprises one or a combination of chemical vapor infiltration (col. 2, lns. 50-55, the forming includes i) fabricating a fiber preform of the airfoil around a plurality of mandrels, wherein the mandrel in the first sub-cavity is radially split, and ii) densifying the fiber preform with a ceramic matrix), melt infiltration, and polymer infiltration and pyrolysis.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102 of this title, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains.  Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
References cited in this section:
D1 - US 2017/0268345 A1
D2 – US 2023/0383657 A1 (filed 27 May 2022)
D3 – US 11,905,847 (filed 21 Oct. 2022)
Claims 9 and 20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over D1 (US 2017/0268345 A1), as applied to claims 1 and 16 above, in view of D2 (US 2023/0383657 A1).
As to claim 9, D1 discloses the  component of claim 8 (see explanation for claim 8), but does not explicitly disclose the following which is taught by D2:
wherein the at least one additional ply (74 in fig. 5) is at least partially disposed within a first platform (74 extends to platform 68 in fig. 5).
It would be obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to use the teachings of D2 for the purpose of configuring fiber plies of the airfoil to facilitate mitigation of stress concentrations and thermal gradients ([0039]-[0044]).
An invention is obvious when created through some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify the prior art reference or to combine prior art reference teachings to arrive at the claimed invention.
As to claim 20, D1 discloses the assembly of claim 19, but does not explicitly disclose the following which is taught by D2: wherein at least one additional ply (74 in fig. 5) is at least partially disposed within the inner diameter platform or the outer diameter platform (74 extends to platform 68 in fig. 5).
It would be obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to use the teachings of D2 for the purpose of configuring fiber plies of the airfoil to facilitate mitigation of stress concentrations and thermal gradients ([0039]-[0044]).
An invention is obvious when created through some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify the prior art reference or to combine prior art reference teachings to arrive at the claimed invention.
Claim 14 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over D3 (US 11,905,847) in view of D2 (US 2023/0383657 A1).
As to claim 14, D3 discloses the method of claim 11 but does not explicitly disclose the following which is taught by D2: laying up at least one platform ply (74) at an angle with respect to the at least one reinforcing ply (72), the at least one reinforcing ply being a projection of the at least one platform ply (74 extends to platform 68).
It would be obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art to use the teachings of D2 for the purpose of configuring fiber plies of the airfoil to facilitate mitigation of stress concentrations and thermal gradients ([0039]-[0044]).
An invention is obvious when created through some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify the prior art reference or to combine prior art reference teachings to arrive at the claimed invention.

Conclusion
The prior art made of record on the attached PTOL-892 and not relied upon is considered pertinent to applicant's disclosure as each further discloses a state of the art.
The examiner has pointed out particular references contained in the prior art of record in the body of this action for the convenience of the applicant. Although the specified citations are representative of the teachings in the art and are applied to the specific limitations within the individual claim, other passages and figures may apply as well. Applicant should consider the entire prior art as applicable as to the limitations of the claims. It is respectfully requested from the applicant, in preparing the response, to consider fully the entire reference as potentially teaching all or part of the claimed invention, as well as the context of the passage as taught by the prior art or pointed out by the examiner.
